text: Once more the printer jams on the same page, so I pull out the crumpled sheet and reseat the tray. Before I can send the report, the screen asks me to choose a driver I have never installed. I click the menu, scroll past three versions, and select the one IT emailed last week.

Each scroll refreshes my spreadsheet, so the cell I just typed vanishes and I retype the same figure. I save the file to the shared folder, and the sync icon spins, then shows an error about a locked file. I close the window, reopen it, and yesterday's numbers are back.

Our video call drops for the third time, and I rejoin with the same link while the host repeats the agenda from the top. My microphone is muted by the app I did not open, so I unmute it and nobody hears the first sentence. I write my point in the chat instead, and it arrives after the vote has closed.

Overnight the shared inbox re-sorts itself, so the client request I flagged sinks under forty newsletters. I drag it to the top of the list, and the next refresh drops it back down. I write the same reply, attach the same file, and press send before the screen times out.

For the second night running, the rice scorches on the bottom of the pot, and the lid rattles when I lift it to check. I add more water, cover it, and turn the flame down to the lowest setting. Twenty minutes later the grains are still hard in the middle and the pan smells burnt.

Bread I slice for lunch tears at every edge, so I toast a fresh piece and the smoke alarm goes off. I wave a tea towel under it, open the back door, and wait while the cheese on the first half sets into a cold lump. I eat it standing at the sink, twenty minutes after I started.

Water for the pasta takes so long to boil that I start the sauce twice. The lid I need is missing from the drawer, so I cover the pot with a plate that slides off every few minutes. When I finally drain the noodles, they clump into one warm mass in the colander.

At the café, the card reader rejects my payment, then the second card, then the phone wallet. The queue behind me shifts its bags, and I dig through my coat for coins I never carry. The barista waves me back to the reader while my latte goes cold on the counter.

A bus I wait for drives past the stop without slowing, so I jog after it to the next light. My transit card shows a zero balance when I tap it, though I topped it up on Sunday. I wait in the rain at the next stop, scrolling my phone for a second route.

Two hundred metres before the exit, the lane I need closes, and cones shove me into a queue that barely moves. Every time I creep forward, the car ahead stops again. I check the sat nav, which reroutes me onto a road that is also closed for resurfacing.

Traffic lights on my route turn red just as I reach them, and the cycle lane ahead is blocked by a delivery van. I crawl up the hill in first gear, then stall at the top with a lorry behind me. The engine restarts only after I roll back and try the hill a second time.

Doors open onto a platform already packed, and the display says the next service is delayed by twelve minutes. I squeeze into the nearest carriage, then get off at the next stop when the doors refuse to close. I follow the signs to the other line, which is shut for engineering works.

Fresh snow has buried the trail markers on the ridge. I retrace my steps to a fork, then lose the faint track again in a stand of pines. My map app shows me exactly where I am, which is still in the middle of nowhere.

Swollen brown after the storm, the creek I planned to cross blocks my route, so I walk upstream looking for stones. Every stone I test shifts under my boot and drops me to the ankle in cold water. By the time I reach the far bank, my socks are soaked and the tent site is still a mile away.

Strawberries have been ripe for a week, but every morning I find the netting pulled off and the beds stripped by something I never see. I rehang the netting with clothes pegs, weighing it down with bricks from the shed. By dusk it has been torn open again.

On this lake, my kayak swings in a slow circle every time I paddle on the left, and the wind pushes me back toward the reeds. I switch sides, dig deeper, and the bow turns again. A rowing pair glides past me, and I am still in the same spot twenty minutes later.

Mid-cycle, the dishwasher stops with a beep, and when I open it the glasses are still gritty. I rinse them by hand, load them again, and press the same button. Halfway through the next cycle, the same beep sounds, and a pool of water spreads across the floor.

Every time I reach the far corner of the rug, the vacuum cord pops out of the socket and the machine shuts off. I plug it back in, climb over the chair legs, and start the strip again. By the time I finish the hall, the dust bin is full and the cord is still in my way.

I scrub the grout line by the tub, and the stain I removed on Monday has returned in a faint grey ring. The cleaner foams, then sinks into the tiles without lifting anything. I rinse, dry, and find a second shadow that wasn't there before.

Wet sheets slide off the line in the gusty yard, so I pin each corner twice with the same two pegs. Then the sky darkens, and the rain starts while the last towel is still dripping on the gravel. I carry the basket back inside and hang everything over the bath.

Under the wrong clinic, my name still shows on the waiting room screen, so the receptionist sends me to another floor. Upstairs the form asks for the same date of birth I typed on the website twice. When the nurse calls me in, she needs to check everything again from the beginning.

Apparently the pharmacy sent my prescription to the old address, so the bag I collect is empty. I call the surgery from the car park, listen to the hold music for eleven minutes, and get disconnected. Tomorrow I will have to start the whole process again.

My physiotherapist asks me to lift the arm slowly, but the shoulder catches halfway every time, the same spot that caught last week. I try the exercise again on the mat while the timer counts down. She notes the progress in her file, though my arm looks no different to me.

Lines on the optician's chart blur when I step back, and the machine clicks through lenses I cannot tell apart. The optician asks which is clearer, and I say the first, then the second, then I am not sure. Then I wait at the desk for a form that never arrives.

My brother's text has the party address, but the link opens a page for a different venue. I call him, and the line cuts out twice before he answers. By the time I find the right place, the cake has been eaten and the guests are leaving.

Dinner with my oldest friend keeps sliding a week later, and each reschedule reaches me through a different app. I reply from the kitchen table, the message fails to send, and I type it again while the kettle boils. We eventually agree on a date, then he calls to cancel it.

Mum asks me to fix her video call again, so I sit beside her on the sofa and tap the green button she has pressed twice already. The camera icon stays grey, the sound cuts to a chirp, and she says the grandchildren can see only the ceiling.

Game night at my friends' flat keeps stalling, because every time we set up the table someone's piece goes missing under the sofa. We restart the scoring twice, then a delivery buzzes the intercom and the cards scatter across the rug.

Halfway through the timed quiz, the online course logs me out, and the answers I typed vanish before the submit button responds. I log back in, scroll to question nine, and see the countdown has already run to zero. The tutor's reply arrives the next morning, asking me to resubmit with an extra form.

Revision cards for the chemistry exam are sorted by topic, but I keep shuffling the stack and losing my place. Each formula I learn slides out of my head before I reach the next card. The highlighter has dried out, so I trace the same equation in pencil, again and again, until the page is grey with smudges.

Our school gate code no longer works, so I stand outside with my bag while the bell rings. Nobody picks up the office phone, so I ring again, then text the class teacher, whose reply sends me the same code that failed. I wait on the step until a parent with a key comes through.

Lecture recordings buffer at the same minute each time, so I restart the video and scrub back to where I was. The library login expires without warning, and I type my student number into a box that has already forgotten me. Then the slides refuse to open, and the file I need is still on my laptop at home.

Among the tall buildings, the running watch cannot find a satellite, so it shows zero pace while my legs keep going. I stop at the gate, restart the app, and wait for the blue ring to fill while the cold sets into my calves. It drops the signal again at the next junction, so I finish the loop on a guess.

Booked for six, my pool lane is taken by a squad of kids who ignore the timetable. I sit on the bench with my goggles in my hand, and the lifeguard says the lane will free up after the lesson. By the time I finally get in, the next group has already claimed the lane.

Between sets, the cable machine sticks at the pin I need, so I unhook the weight and rethread it. Someone takes the bench I was about to use, and I wait again with chalk drying on my palms. The next set fails at the same rep, because the bar is still set for someone taller.

Across the river, the footbridge on my mapped route is closed for works, so I double back past three dead ends. Each detour adds another hill I did not plan for, and my intervals keep stopping at the crossing lights. By the end of the hour I have run less than half the distance I set out to cover.

Last weekend's shelf bracket is the wrong size, and the wall plugs crumble when I drill the second hole. I measure again, level the bracket, and the bubble drifts off-centre as soon as I tighten the screw. The bookcase tips slightly every time I lean a book against it.

Snagged yarn on the stitch I dropped sends me back three rows to find it. Each time I restart the pattern, the cable twists the wrong way and I have to start the sleeve again. By evening the needles still click, and I have not finished the cuff.

Hinge screws strip out of the cabinet door before the second one goes in, so I drill a larger hole and find the dowel has split. I add glue, wait an hour, and the door still sags an inch when I let go.

Clay on my wheel slumps every time I centre it, and the bowl collapses into a lopsided ring. I wet my hands, add water, and try again with less pressure. Three attempts later the walls tear under my thumb.

Every ten minutes the post office queue shifts one person forward, and the clerk stops to check every parcel label. When my turn comes, the scale says my box is two grams over the limit, so I unpack and repack it on the counter.

Self-checkout reads my cucumber as a banana, and the attendant has to come over and override it. The bag I packed tips on the scanner, and loose apples roll under the gap. I check the receipt twice, and the total is still higher than the shelf price.

After the third wrong code, the bank app locks my card, and the branch can only reopen it tomorrow. I walk to the cash machine across the road and find it out of order, a handwritten sign taped to the screen. The taxi home takes the long way round, and I have no cash left for the fare.

Harsh lights make the changing room mirror show the jacket one size too small, and the sizes on the rack are missing the one I need. I ask the assistant to check the stockroom, and she returns with a different colour. The online version I order that night arrives in the wrong size too.

Three flights down, my suitcase bumps every step, because the hotel key card stops working at the lift. At reception, the clerk reprograms it, but the card fails again before I reach my door. Then I climb the stairs a fourth time, the case heavier with every landing.

Twice in forty minutes the gate changes, and each time the departures board shows a new time for the same flight. I queue at the desk for a rebooking that offers only a seat in the middle row, then the desk screen freezes and my booking reference disappears.

Out of date, the ferry timetable I printed sends me to the pier twenty minutes after the last crossing has left. The website says the next one runs at four, but the ticket office has closed, and the chalkboard still shows noon. I sit on my rucksack by the bins, scrolling for a coach to a town with a station.

Trusting the rental car's GPS, I drive down a track that ends at a locked gate, so I reverse a long way back to the junction. I reset the route, and the voice announces the same lane as the best option. Back at the junction my phone has no signal, so the map stays frozen on the same blue dot.

Each pass through the bridge, the E above middle C sticks and the melody stalls on the same note. I lift the lid, press it again, and the hammer answers a half-second late. The metronome keeps clicking through my mistakes, and I keep stopping to start from bar one.

Watercolour bleeds across the paper whatever I do, and the sky turns into a muddy grey wash. I blot it, let it dry, and paint over the same patch while the light fades. By the time the paint sets, the clouds look like a stain.

Tiny decals for the model train peel as I lift one, fold over themselves, and tear at the edge. I soak it, press it flat with a cotton bud, and it wrinkles across the carriage roof. The second decal goes on at the wrong angle, and the paint around the window has cracked.

Rehearsal stalls on the same bar for the fourth Thursday running, because the altos keep coming in a beat early. I count the rests under my breath, but the conductor stops us at the bar again. The piano keeps returning to bar nine, and nobody mentions the altos.

A laptop update restarts itself in the middle of my document, and the autosave misses the last paragraph. I reopen the file, retype the lost section, and the spellcheck underlines the same typo it underlined before. Ten minutes later the Wi-Fi drops, and the document refuses to sync.

Storage is full once more and the photo app asks me to free space before I can take a single picture. I delete a hundred photos this week, but the trash folder fills up again, and the backup icon spins without finishing. Each deleted file seems to come back by morning.

Offline, my laptop's software licence check fails, so I connect it to the hotspot and the activation server times out. I try the backup key from the email, which the system rejects because it has already been used. The support form asks me to describe the problem, so I type the same sentence into three separate fields.

Joining my own meeting means updating the video call app first, and the update bar stalls at forty-one percent. I reboot the phone, sign in again, and the code sent to my number never arrives. The meeting starts without me while I wait by the window.
